entry.title: Installing Nexus and Artifactory Proxies
entry.summary: The motivation is to both make build faster and more reliable due to less network latency. Also
entry.content:
The motivation is to both make build faster and more reliable due to less network latency. Also to avoid issues with the availability of some external resources over time, either due to network access policies or their deprecation.

Nexus​

The free version of Nexus is able to host NPM repositories proxies, so I use it for React and Angular frontends.

Installation in Proxmox VM​

On Proxmox Nexus VM ran:

sudo docker run -d  \
   -p 8081:8081 \
   --name nexus \
   --restart always \
   -v nexus-data:/nexus-data \
  sonatype/nexus3:latest

Copied the autogenerated password to use for the first login in Nexus Web UI:

sudo docker exec -it nexus cat /nexus-data/admin.password

Created a remote repository named npm-proxy and added the repository URL to Jenkins credentials as a text note.

Jenkins Pipeline​

Added the URL to the Jenkins pipeline as an argument to Docker build, for example:

Jenkinsfile
stage('Build Docker Images') {
  steps {
    withCredentials([
      string(credentialsId: 'NEXUS_NPM_URL', variable: 'NEXUS_NPM_URL')
    ]) {
      sh """
        docker build \
          . -t money.tracker.ui -f Dockerfile \
          --build-arg="ENVIRONMENT=uat" \
          --build-arg="NPM_REGISTRY=${NEXUS_NPM_URL}"
      """
    }
  }
}

Nx Angular Project​

Once Docker gets the URL, it will use it to configure the fetching of packages regardless of packages resolution information contained in package-lock.json file:

COPY .babelrc eslint.config.mjs decorate-angular-cli.js \
     jest.config.ts jest.preset.js nx.json postcss.config.json .postcssrc.json \
     package.json package-lock.json tsconfig.base.json ./

ARG NPM_REGISTRY=https://registry.npmjs.org/
ENV NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY="${NPM_REGISTRY}"

RUN npm ci  --no-audit --no-fund

So the project files themselves are not modified in any way.

note

The Angular project has pretty modestly counted towards 1,413 artifacts out of 40,000 free usage limits. The number of requests a build made was about 5,000, which is acceptable since it is allowed to make 100 thousand requests per day, which gives about 20 free builds.

Artifactory​

The OSS version of Artifactory doesn't support npm packages, so I installed it to proxy Java repositories.

Installation in Proxmox VM​

Created a unique MASTER_KEY with:

export MASTER_KEY=$(openssl rand -hex 16)

There should be jfrog/artifactory/var and jfrog/postgres/data directories created for Artifactory and Postgres data:

anton@artifactory:~$ ls -l
total 20
-rw-rw-r-- 1 anton anton 1121 Apr  2  2026 docker-compose.yml
drwxrwxr-x 4 anton anton 4096 Apr  2  2026 jfrog

On Proxmox Nexus VM created a docker-compose file:

services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:15-alpine
    container_name: postgres
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: artifactory
      POSTGRES_USER: artifactory
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U artifactory -d artifactory"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5
    volumes:
      - ~/jfrog/postgres/data:/var/lib/postgresql/data

  artifactory:
    image: releases-docker.jfrog.io/jfrog/artifactory-oss:latest
    container_name: artifactory
    depends_on:
      postgres:
        condition: service_healthy
    ports:
      - "8081:8081"
      - "8082:8082"
    environment:
      JF_SHARED_DATABASE_TYPE: postgresql
      JF_SHARED_DATABASE_DRIVER: org.postgresql.Driver
      JF_SHARED_DATABASE_URL: jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/artifactory
      JF_SHARED_DATABASE_USERNAME: artifactory
      JF_SHARED_DATABASE_PASSWORD: password
      JF_SHARED_SECURITY_MASTERKEY: 5b54a897974e51c087826ba34ae22350
      JF_JFCONNECT_ENABLED: "false"
      JF_SHARED_NODE_IP: "192.168.1.174"
    volumes:
      - ~/jfrog/artifactory/var:/opt/jfrog/var

Started both services with Docker Compose:

docker compose up -d

Created remote repositories named maven-proxy and gradle-plugins-remote, generated a key for the repository with the 'Set Me Up' function, for example, cmVmd... and added it with the repository URL to Jenkins credentials as text notes. The key can be revoked in the Artifactory UI as well.

Gradle Project​

For local Gradle development it is possible to tell Gradle to use the credentials by placing them into the local gradle.properties file, which should not be checked into version control:

gradle.properties
artifactory_user=admin
artifactory_password=cmVmd...

The repositories' management is best done in settings.gradle, for example:

settings.gradle
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories {
        // Check if the pipeline explicitly requested Artifactory
        def useArtifactory = System.getenv("USE_ARTIFACTORY") == "true"
        if (useArtifactory) {
            maven {
                url "http://192.168.1.174:8082/artifactory/gradle-plugins-remote"
                allowInsecureProtocol = true
                credentials {
                    username = providers.gradleProperty("artifactory_user").orNull ?: System.getenv("ARTIFACTORY_USER")
                    password = providers.gradleProperty("artifactory_password").orNull ?: System.getenv("ARTIFACTORY_PASSWORD")
                }
            }
            maven {
                url = System.getenv("ARTIFACTORY_MAVEN_URL")
                allowInsecureProtocol = true
                credentials {
                    username = providers.gradleProperty("artifactory_user").orNull ?: System.getenv("ARTIFACTORY_USER")
                    password = providers.gradleProperty("artifactory_password").orNull ?: System.getenv("ARTIFACTORY_PASSWORD")
                }
            }
        } else {
            // Fallback for GitHub Actions
            mavenCentral()
        }
    }
}

The Artifactory URL can be not hidden with Jenkins credentials, it is not a secret either. The switcher here is USE_ARTIFACTORY environment variable. If it is not set, Gradle will use the Maven Central repository, like in the case of GitHub Actions builds.

Jenkins Pipeline​

The following lines will wrap the Gradle build:

stage('Gradle Build') {
    steps {
        withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'artifactory-admin-token',
                                         passwordVariable: 'ARTIFACTORY_PASSWORD',
                                         usernameVariable: 'ARTIFACTORY_USER')]) {
            withEnv(['USE_ARTIFACTORY=true']) {
                sh './gradlew clean build'
            }
        }
    }
}

And the example local build:

export USE_ARTIFACTORY=true & ./gradlew clean build

entry.title: Money Tracker UI with Storage API
entry.summary: Added a significantly renovated design plus integration with Clematis Storage API gives
entry.content:
Added a significantly renovated design plus integration with Clematis Storage API gives a persistent storage for commodities, organizations and accounts main images.

The images themselves can be simply pasted from the clipboard in a new image uploader component, this makes the authoring of entity front image easier:

  1. Paste the image from the clipboard, scale and move it to the desired position. The uploader will crop the visible area of the image.
  1. Clicking the "Save" button will upload the image to the Clematis Storage API and will display the resulting image in the read-only uploader. In this example the image has been scaled down before upload if compared with the first screenshot.

The component sources can be found here.

entry.title: Jenkins Migration to Java 25 LTS
entry.summary: My Turnkey Jenkins LXC stopped updates via apt a month ago, and here are my notes on how to fix it.
entry.content:
My Turnkey Jenkins LXC stopped updates via apt a month ago, and here are my notes on how to fix it.

I had to update the key first:

curl -fsSL https://pkg.jenkins.io/debian/jenkins.io-2026.key | sudo tee /usr/share/keyrings/jenkins-keyring.asc > /dev/null

And to update the repository:

echo "deb [signed-by=/usr/share/keyrings/jenkins-keyring.asc] https://pkg.jenkins.io/debian-stable binary/" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/jenkins.list

Also, Jenkins needs Java 21 or higher. Installing it via deb package (Zulu):

sudo dpkg -i zulu25.32.17-ca-jdk25.0.2-linux_amd64.deb

In case any dependencies are missing, install them:

sudo apt --fix-broken install -y

Finally, fix the jenkins service path:

nano /lib/systemd/system/jenkins.service

Change

ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /usr/share/jenkins/jenkins.war`

to

ExecStart=/usr/bin/java -jar /usr/share/java/jenkins.war

Reload systemd:

sudo systemctl daemon-reload

entry.title: Clematis Desktop Plugins Installer
entry.summary: The next update for Clematis Desktop includes a new version of Runtime Manager UI plugin enriched
entry.content:
The next update for Clematis Desktop includes a new version of Runtime Manager UI plugin enriched with plugin downloader and installer, plus some more JVM monitors with GC marks.

There are many ideas yet to be implemented; the current list of changes is as follows:

  1. Removed Kiwi Plugin 'expected' type.
  2. Kiwi Plugin type control: ANY type can be loaded as SYSTEM or USER types of plugins, otherwise the types have to match
  3. Replaced the plugin list with the plugin table in Runtime Manager UI
  4. Fixed Kiwi Plugin classloader resource bundle issue
  5. Improved layout of the monitors' section
  6. Improved layout of the tabbed pane
  7. New type of UI extension shells that are loaded as USER plugins but are common for all users. Their lifecycle is slightly different from the one of SYSTEM plugins, since these shells are being destroyed at the end of each user session.
  8. Plugin download from a URL and automatic installation afterward
  9. Plugin uninstallation buttons
  10. New log panel component

entry.title: Clematis Desktop Java 21 & Refactoring
entry.summary: Clematis Desktop
entry.content:
Clematis Desktop is updated to work with Java version 21. There were a few steps were made:

  • Gradle is updated to 9.1.0
  • Changes in build files syntax to support Gradle 9.1.0

The project gradually accepts new language features as much of the old code is being refactored, for example, to remove the lengthy Desktop class and break down its functionality into smaller classes, organized in a more Java Swing way. More details are available in the README.
